html:
SWE Simulator (swesim): design spec, v2.1

Date: 2026-09-12 (v2.1, after the Codex adversarial review in docs/reviews/2026-09-12-codex-adversarial-review.md and the second review in docs/reviews/2026-09-12-claude-adversarial-review-v2.md). Status: for review. Author: Saahil Sanganeriya, with Claude. v1 is archived beside this file.

0. What changed from v1

Blocking fixes: reward.json is numeric-only with a separate report.json (B1); the agent's working tree is collected by a root-owned tar collect hook into a root-only directory, after the agent's processes are killed, under the allowlist baseline, with no git or agent code execution (B2, and BL1 of the second review); any control designated an incorrect exploit must score zero or the task is rejected (B3). Second-review fixes: session freeze happens in the collect hook and its transcript hash is bound into the receipt (BL2); outcomes are keyed on success, not reward (BL3); startup hooks (sitecustomize.py, usercustomize.py, *.pth) are protected and pytest runs in isolated mode (MA1); the report-path-secrecy claim is dropped and in-process forgery is stated as residual with a stdout cross-check (MA2); hook user pinned to root (MA3); disclosure granularity rule and questions-conditioned reporting (MA4); two-tailed calibration screen and existence-demonstration framing (MA5, ED5); pool A only for the first version (MA6); dashboard reduced to a runs table plus a post-hoc episode page with near-live chat polling, no Temporal visibility integration, no live agent stream (MA8, MA9); schedule cut to one model tier first (MA10); mini-swe-agent as the agent user verified by spike (MA11); spike evidence attached under references/modal-smoke-task/spike-results/ (MI3, MI4). Major fixes: one topology (Modal single-container, hosted stakeholder, separate verifier, transcript joined on the worker) (M1); full brief excludes author-only material by construction (M2); hardened record with asset manifest, run config, excerpt provenance, and strict validation (M3, M7, N4); base and gold expected-status evidence (M4); attribution rules for outcomes (M5); stakeholder session protocol (M6); simulator labeled stochastic, labels adjudicated by humans in the pilot (M8); frozen budgets and diff-only review for all compared runs (M9, M10); path policy at patch application (M11); calibration separated from comparison (M12); tracked example task (M13); episode manifest export (M14); bounded repo-only discovery (M15); Temporal kept thin with stable trial ids and no automatic launch retries (M16, M17, N5); positioning corrected (N1); counts qualified (N2). Cut list applied (section 2).

1. Thesis

SWE-bench hands an agent the issue text as the reporter wrote it and grades a patch with the fix's tests. Many of those issues are underspecified; the hints_text discussion exists in the dataset but is not shown to the agent. SWE-bench Verified removed instances whose issue was rated underspecified or whose tests were rated unfair. DeepSWE and Terminal-Bench author fully specified instructions. In all of them there is nobody to ask.

swesim keeps the underspecified issue as the brief, puts the resolution with a simulated stakeholder the agent can talk to, and grades with the fix's tests in a clean container. The product is a pipeline that produces such tasks from two sources for the first version, SWE-bench's human-annotated underspecified instances and any GitHub repository URL, packaged as Harbor tasks, run on Modal, orchestrated by Temporal, and inspectable per episode.

2. Scope for the first version and non-goals

In scope by the presentation, in critical-path order:

  1. The separate verifier with path policy, expected-test manifest, numeric reward, report, and outcome attribution, exercised by real controls on one SWE-bench task (sections 9, 10).
  2. The stakeholder service with the session protocol, the limited tool loop (read_diff, read_changed_file, and run_check in a Modal Sandbox), exercised by one interactive episode with a real agent (section 8). If run_check is not working by the morning of 09-13, compared runs use diff-only and say so.
  3. The full swebench-annotated path: mine, judge, spec (human-edited), compile to three conditions, validate, register, run, score, export, on a task that passes the non-derivability requirement (section 6).
  4. The github-repo path from a repository URL with bounded discovery, one task discovered, built, validated and run through the same stages.
  5. Temporal orchestration, thin: one pipeline workflow, one trial workflow, persistent dev server on the VM, worker under systemd.
  6. Tracked example task package and one sanitized example run in the repo.
  7. Dashboard: a runs table and an episode page with near-live stakeholder chat by polling and the full interleaved episode after completion (section 17), plus harbor view and the Temporal UI.
  8. README, grading document, architecture and realism document.

Model configurations for the pilot: two, one weaker tier and one frontier tier, k = 3 attempts, three conditions. Expansion to more tiers only after everything above exists.

Non-goals for the first version: DeepSWE, SWE-bench Pro, SWE-rebench importers; Trac fetcher; stakeholder source-debugging tools; multi-step episodes; Harbor's native user-agent bridge; GKE; Temporal Cloud; GCS auto-sync (an export command and durable job directories suffice); automated semantic failure labeling; four polished dashboard screens; any claim that a model has not seen a task.

3. Prior art and positioning

Work What it does What it leaves for us
SWE-bench Issue text to patch; FAIL_TO_PASS and PASS_TO_PASS; ships hints_text but does not show it to the agent no interlocutor; underspecified issues are unsolvable by design
SWE-bench Verified Human filter on underspecification and test fairness; 500 kept of 1,699 annotated the rejected instances and their human notes
Ambig-SWE (Vijayvargiya et al., ICLR 2026) A benchmark variant of Verified with information removed by an LLM summary, plus a simulated user given the full issue, hints and file locations we start from issues humans rated underspecified, remove by category with each removal recorded as a ledger fact, keep the natural brief for measurement, and give the stakeholder provenance-tagged knowledge without file locations
Ask or Assume? (Edwards and Schuster, 2026) Agent-side clarification scaffold on that variant; Full 70.8 vs Hidden 54.8 for Sonnet 4.5 in its setup environment-side pipeline, grading integrity
tau-bench (Sierra) LLM user with hidden scenario, final-state reward, pass^k domain transfer to code
DeepSWE v1.1 (2026) Harbor tasks, separate verifier, collected patch, stripped git history, per-test reports interaction; generation from public threads
SWE-Gym (real PRs) and SWE-smith (procedural modification), R2E-Gym Task generation at scale naturally underspecified briefs with a grounded interlocutor
Harbor 0.23 Task format, 44 registered agents, viewer, native user bridge (claude-code and gemini-cli targets only, not with multi-step) the stakeholder protocol and grading contract

Our contribution, stated narrowly: an authoring and validation workflow that turns naturally underspecified issues with human labels into interactive tasks whose stakeholder holds excerpt-backed facts, graded by a verifier whose controls are executed and recorded. No categorical novelty claim.

4. Architecture

 sources:  swebench-annotated | github-repo | (authored: interface only)
              │
              ▼
 Temporal PipelineWorkflow ─ activities: mine → judge → draft_spec → [signal: human approves] → compile → validate → register
              │                                    (all read/write the workspace; ScenarioSpec is the only handoff after draft_spec)
              ▼
 Temporal TrialWorkflow(trial_id) ─ activities: ensure_session → launch_harbor (no retry) → await_result → fetch_transcript → score → export
              │
              ▼
 Harbor (modal backend): [agent sandbox] ──tar of /app──▶ [separate verifier] ──reward.json/report.json──▶ job dir
        agent sandbox ◀──HTTPS (allowlisted)──▶ [stakeholder service on Modal]  ──transcript──▶ fetched by worker, joined by trial_id

One topology. The stakeholder transcript is never an agent artifact; the worker fetches it from the service after the trial and stores it beside the Harbor result. Everything after draft_spec consumes only the validated ScenarioSpec plus a versioned RunConfig.

5. The normalized record

5.1 ScenarioSpec (per scenario, versioned, strict)

Pydantic model with extra="forbid". Validators reject: duplicate fact or requirement ids; dangling references; empty fail_to_pass; empty oracle diff; missing natural brief; ids not matching ^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9._-]{2,63}$; author-only facts with test links; facts without excerpt or authored rationale; asset references not present in the manifest.

  • id, version (>= 1), source, source_ref, created_at, pipeline_version, spec_hash (computed over the canonical JSON).
  • environment: kind (prebuilt-image | dockerfile); for prebuilt-image, image and image_digest (resolved at compile); for dockerfile, dockerfile_asset (manifest ref) and build_context_assets; repo_url, base_commit, language, test_command, install_notes.
  • assets: manifest {name: {path, sha256, bytes}}, paths relative to the scenario directory; covers hidden test files, protected-path overlays, reproducer files, control patches, the Dockerfile.
  • briefs: [{profile, text, provenance}]. Three profiles:
    • natural (required): the issue exactly as filed, provenance original-issue.
    • withheld (decided 2026-09-12, default interactive brief when present): a model-produced version of the natural issue with specific categories removed, never a free summary. Removable categories: reproduction code and commands, error messages and tracebacks, literal expected outputs, file, function and line references, version pins, and explicit "the fix is" proposals. The brief must keep a recognizable symptom or request, enough context to begin, and the desired outcome. Every removed span becomes a ledger fact with provenance: original-issue, source_excerpt equal to the removed text verbatim, source_url the issue, discovery: on-request (or repo-derivable when the agent can recover it from the code, such as a file location), and an operations entry of type withholding. Provenance of the profile is withheld. Code checks at approve that none of the withheld excerpts appear in the withheld brief and that the title's symptom words are retained.
    • other authored profiles (for example title-only) are optional difficulty variants. Lossiness is therefore selected for (the natural issue is already rated underspecified) and then extended in a recorded, reversible way. The natural brief is always kept so the effect of withholding is measured (section 11), never assumed.
  • ledger: [Fact] with id, text, kind (behavior | interface | constraint | reproduction | context), provenance (issue-thread | pr-thread | pr-review | annotator-note | authored), source_excerpt and source_url (required unless authored, then authored_rationale required), discovery (brief | on-request | volunteered-at-review | repo-derivable | author-only), tests (contract test ids; must be empty for author-only).
  • operations: [{type: clarification | evaluator-repair | synthetic-extension | withholding, target, rationale}], one entry for every change relative to the historical material; withholding entries name the fact ids moved from the brief to the ledger.
  • persona: {summary, tone, disclosure_style, derived_from_urls}.
  • requirements: [{id, text, fact_id?, tests, source_url}], mined from review; used by the stakeholder's review reply; never replayed verbatim.
  • contract: fail_to_pass, pass_to_pass (exact test ids), test_assets (manifest refs for files the verifier owns), protected_paths (globs whose changes are never applied, see 10.2), expected_base and expected_gold (per-test statuses recorded by validate), runner (command template producing JUnit XML).
  • checks: predefined stakeholder reproducer checks [{id, description, command, asset?, expected_observation}], disjoint from the contract tests; derived from the reporter's reproducer or ordinary user workflows.
  • controls: oracle (asset), plausible_wrong (>= 1, each with rationale, expected_success: 0 and expected_reward_max), alternative_correct (>= 1 when the judge flags structural tests, else optional, expected_success: 1), tamper (>= 1 of class incorrect-exploit with expected_reward: 0; optional benign-edit class with expected_success: 1 and expected signals).
  • groups: requirement groups for partial credit (10.5): {id, weight, tests} covering every FAIL_TO_PASS id exactly once.
  • difficulty: annotated, judged (score, rationale, model id, prompt version), measured (filled by score, keyed by run config hash).
  • thread: cached discussion with URLs, redacted of the gold diff.

5.2 RunConfig (per run, versioned, hashed)

agent (Harbor agent name, version), model (provider id), condition, brief_profile (withheld if the scenario has one, else natural; applies to hidden and interactive), solver_timeout_sec, stakeholder (model_id, prompt_version, temperature, patience_profile (section 8), review_mode: checks | diff-only, max_tool_calls_per_activation), k, harbor_version, environment_provider: modal, run_config_hash. Every trial id embeds it: trial_id = h(spec_hash, condition, run_config_hash, attempt_index).

6. Sources

Priority set by Saahil: SWE-bench annotated pool first, GitHub repository URL second, DeepSWE a bonus after both work (not in trial scope).

Source Input natural brief Ledger provenance Environment Trial status
swebench-annotated pool letter, optional instance ids problem_statement verbatim issue-thread (hints_text plus GitHub API), pr-thread, pr-review; annotator-note only when corroborated by the thread, else authored prebuilt swebench/sweb.eval.x86_64.<id>, digest resolved at compile primary
github-repo repository URL; optional --pr N issue body same, all from GitHub API Dockerfile built by the pipeline at the PR base commit primary
authored scenario directory human or LLM text authored any interface only

Pools for swebench-annotated (exact predicates over the ensembled CSV, other_major_issues == 0 throughout): A: underspecified >= 2 and false_negative <= 1 (109); B: underspecified >= 2 and false_negative == 2 (245); C: underspecified <= 1 and false_negative == 2 (276). Pool A is the trial pool. Reading pool B's test-validity notes shows most describe test overfitting (evaluator defects), so a pool B instance is admitted only with a human-written justification that the withheld fact is a genuine product decision and that the FAIL_TO_PASS tests do not encode an arbitrary implementation detail; where a test does, the operation is recorded as evaluator-repair and that test is excluded from the scored contract. 539 rows pass the published filter and 500 are in Verified; pools are defined by scores, not by set difference. django instances are deprioritized (Trac tracker).

Non-derivability requirement (added after review of the SymPy Mod example, which a strong model solves from mathematics alone): a candidate is kept for the interactive set only if at least one contract-required fact is a choice among reasonable alternatives that neither the repository nor domain knowledge determines: which exception type, which of two output shapes, whether to warn or raise, what to do for an input the reporter could not share, which public name to expose. The judge records this fact and its alternatives. Facts a capable engineer could infer from the code or the domain are tagged repo-derivable and do not qualify. Non-derivability alone does not make a good task: prefer missing decisions with engineering consequences (backward compatibility, failure handling, output semantics, migration behavior) over arbitrary strings such as an exact message that is unknowable but inconsequential. Empirical screen: after calibration runs (k as large as budget allows, at least 3), a task the frontier tier passes in hidden on all attempts (underspecification not load-bearing) or fails in full on all attempts (unsolvable even with the information) is moved out of the comparison set and kept as a calibration record.

Pool A skews small (measured 2026-09-12 over the 109 gold patches: median 6 source additions in one file, 90th percentile 32, maximum 189 in sympy): underspecified issues whose tests survived the fairness filter are mostly small bug fixes. Pool A is therefore the right first source for proving the interaction mechanism on prebuilt environments, not for demonstrating complex implementation; prefer its 1-to-4-hour instances, and take complexity from the github-repo feature band. This screen selects on the dependent variable; the comparison set is therefore reported as a calibrated, biased sample with the thresholds stated, and results are an existence demonstration, not a measured gradient. Prefer annotated difficulty above fifteen minutes and multi-file fixes.

Annotator notes describe both missing intent and evaluator defects; a note is never a fact's sole provenance. If a thread references a reproducer that is not publicly available, the candidate is rejected or the reconstruction is marked authored with rationale.

github-repo discovery, bounded: parameters --since, --max-prs (default 400), --max-candidates (default 20), --max-builds (default 3), --build-profile python-pytest (the only supported profile: Python package installable with uv pip install -e . or the repo's declared extras, tests run with pytest), and --kind bugfix|feature (default feature). Steps: list merged PRs in the window; resolve linked issues from PR body keywords and issue timeline cross-references; keep pairs where the PR changes both source and test files, the source diff is within the kind's band, the issue plus PR thread has at least --min-comments non-bot comments, and the issue predates the PR; fetch threads; write candidates.jsonl with a reason per reject.

Complexity bands (decided 2026-09-12 after measuring 6458 merged PRs since 2025-09-01 across the 12 SWE-bench repos and the 91 DeepSWE upstream repos: additions p50 28, p90 450, p99 5264; 71 PRs above 5,000 lines, all migrations, generated code, docs or release rollups; details and the per-repo ranking in docs/notes/2026-09-12-target-repos.md):

kind source additions source files thread comments issue labels preferred
bugfix 20 to 300 1 to 10 >= 4 bug
feature 200 to 1,500 3 to 30 >= 8 enhancement, feature, RFC, proposal

"Complex enough" means the feature band: a feature request or RFC whose design (API shape, defaults, backward compatibility, error semantics) was negotiated in review. Line count above that band is not pursued: very large PRs are migrations, generated or vendored code, and their tests cover a sliver of the change. Very long horizons of the CodeClash kind (15 rounds of up to 30 turns, goal-oriented competition without a fixed spec) are a different research question and out of scope. If no candidate survives, the workflow ends in no-valid-candidate with the reject histogram. Environment build: clone at base, install, run the PR's test files once and require that at least one fails on base and passes after the gold patch; then strip history (9.3). Build failures are recorded per candidate and count against --max-builds.

7. Pipeline stages

Each stage is a plain Python function stage(workspace, id, run_config?) -> StageResult writing files under workspace/<scenario_id>/ and a small JSON result. Temporal activities wrap them; swesim <stage> --direct calls them without Temporal.

  1. mine: as in section 6. Output candidates.jsonl.

  2. judge: LLM rubric with fixed prompt version over issue, thread, diff, tests; scores complexity, spec gap, test behavioralness, self-containment; answers the four questions (what is missing; does the thread supply it; is it a legitimate behavioral requirement; does the evaluator accept alternative correct implementations). Output judged.jsonl. A prior, not a difficulty measure.

    How underspecification is detected without human annotators (the github-repo source), most to least objective: (a) the issue-to-contract delta, extracted by code: exception class names and string literals asserted in the test patch, new public names introduced by the gold patch, and behavioral branches visible in the diff that the issue text never mentions; the judge classifies each candidate gap, never the issue as a whole, on four questions: derivable from the repository, consequential for callers, resolved by a stakeholder statement in the thread or only by the patch, and category; a candidate is accepted only if at least one gap is non-derivable, consequential and stakeholder-resolved, and that list is also the menu for the withheld brief; the judge model differs from the draft model so their errors are not correlated, and prompt version and model id are recorded in difficulty.judged; (b) thread evidence: maintainer questions in the issue before the PR and reviewer-requested behavior or interface changes; (c) the Verified rubric itself: the judge scores underspecification 0 to 3 using the annotators' published instructions, and swesim judge-calibrate --n 150 measures its agreement with the 1,699 human labels on a held-out sample at the severity-2 threshold before the judge is used on new repositories; the agreement figure is reported in the grading document; (d) the empirical hidden screen (section 6). With the withheld brief profile, the judge's main output is the list of facts in the issue that are decisions with engineering consequences, which are the candidates for withholding.

  3. draft_spec: LLM drafts ScenarioSpec with excerpts; drafts control patches; produces the withheld brief and its withheld facts by category, with the leak check run in code. Output scenario.draft.json. The workflow then waits for the approve_spec signal carrying the human-edited JSON, or times out into awaiting-approval. The human edit is the authoring step and is recorded.

  4. compile: validates the spec, resolves image digest, emits three Harbor task directories, writes compile.json with hashes.

  5. validate: runs controls through Harbor on Modal once per spec version (the contract is identical across conditions): base expected statuses via nop (must show every F2P failing and every P2P passing, recorded as expected_base), oracle (expected_gold, reward 1, success 1), each plausible-wrong (success 0 and reward at most its declared maximum), each alternative-correct (success 1), each tamper (incorrect-exploit must earn reward 0; benign-edit must succeed with its expected signals). Any mismatch marks the scenario invalid with the failing control. Output validation.json.

  6. register: appends to registry.json and Harbor dataset.toml with version, hashes, validation status, asset paths.

  7. run: per TrialWorkflow, launches harbor run for one trial id; on completion fetches the stakeholder transcript by trial id; stores both.

  8. score: per scenario and run config: outcome classes, pass@k and pass^k computed by swesim over attempts using success (Harbor's own helper requires a single binary key and is not used), mean partial reward, code-exact interaction counts (questions, reviews, patience end, whether the last reviewed diff equals the submitted patch), and a field for human-adjudicated labels.

  9. export: writes the episode manifest (section 16).

  10. view: serves the dashboard (section 17).

7a. Orchestration with Temporal (thin)

  • Server: temporal server start-dev --db-filename /var/lib/swesim/temporal.db --ip 0.0.0.0 on the GCE VM under systemd; UI on 8233 via SSH tunnel.
  • Worker: one process, task queue swesim, activity concurrency 4, launch concurrency 2 (Modal jobs), under systemd with restart.
  • PipelineWorkflow(source, params): activities mine, then per candidate judge, draft_spec, wait for approve_spec signal (timeout 24h), compile, validate, register. Fan-out bounded by --max-candidates.
  • TrialWorkflow(trial_id): workflow id equals trial_id, so a second start is rejected by Temporal and a trial cannot be launched twice by a retry of the parent. Activities: ensure_session (idempotent, keyed by trial id), launch_harbor (retry policy: maximum attempts 1; on failure the trial is marked launch-failed and reported), await_result (heartbeating poll of the job directory), fetch_transcript, score, export. A new experimental attempt is a new attempt_index, never a Temporal retry.
  • Payloads carry ids and hashes only; files stay in the workspace.
  • Restart check before the presentation: kill the worker mid-trial and confirm exactly one recorded attempt after recovery.

8. The stakeholder service

Form (decided 2026-09-12, revised after discussion): a limited, event-driven agent, cooperative about requirements and limited about implementation. It is activated by events (ask, review) and runs a small bounded tool loop (at most 4 tool calls per activation) before replying. Its tools are code-controlled and read-only:

  • read_diff(): the diff submitted with the current review request.
  • read_changed_file(path): a file from the submitted snapshot, only for paths present in the diff.
  • run_check(check_id): one of the scenario's predefined reproducer checks (user-level workflows or the reporter's reproducer, never the hidden contract tests), executed in an isolated Modal Sandbox built from the task image with the submitted diff applied, no network, no secrets, bounded time and output. Returns observed behavior and output.

Four boundaries: knowledge (stakeholder-visible view only; no oracle, no hidden tests); tools (the three above; no editing, no shell, no source debugging); feedback (expected versus observed behavior and requirement clarifications; never prescribed edits or algorithms, enforced by prompt and audited in the transcript); availability (the patience budget, identical across compared runs). The stakeholder's "looks good" is feedback, not reward. Every tool call and its result is recorded in the transcript and shown on the trial page beside the reply, so a reviewer can judge whether the stakeholder clarified or effectively solved.

Review modes, frozen per RunConfig and identical across compared runs: checks (tools available, the default once run_check works) or diff-only (only read_diff and read_changed_file; replies state that nothing was executed). Prior art: SWE-Interact gives its simulated user tools to inspect the workspace; our difference is evidence-backed generation of the stakeholder's knowledge and inspectability of its actions.

Hosted on Modal as a web endpoint, one deployment, many sessions. Holds per session: the stakeholder-visible view of the spec (facts with discovery in {brief, on-request, volunteered-at-review, repo-derivable}, persona, requirements; never author-only facts, never the oracle, never test files), the RunConfig stakeholder block, budgets, counters, and the transcript.

Session protocol:

  • POST /sessions (worker only, authenticated by a worker secret): body {trial_id, spec_hash, condition, run_config_hash}; returns a session token bound to the trial id. hidden and full conditions get no session.
  • POST /ask and POST /review (agent, via shims, session token, and a client request_id): requests for one session are serialized; a repeated request_id returns the cached reply; counters are server-owned; over budget returns a fixed refusal. Replies record generated_at, delivered: true on successful HTTP response.
  • POST /freeze (session token): closes the session; later requests get 410; returns transcript_hash. It is called by the root collect hook after the agent's processes are killed and before the verifier starts (Harbor stops the agent container before the separate verifier runs, and the worker only regains control after harbor run returns, so the worker cannot freeze at that point). The hash is written into the collection receipt; the worker later fetches the transcript by trial id and checks it.
  • The LLM context contains only the stakeholder-visible view; author-only and evaluator material are excluded structurally, not by instruction.

Disclosure policy: any on-request fact may be given when a related question is asked, at the level of specificity asked. A broad question ("what exactly do you need?") receives the requirement list at requirement level; specific facts such as an exact exception type or message need a specific question. No forced drip beyond that granularity rule, which mirrors how a maintainer answers "what do you want?" versus "which exception?". Because a single broad question can still unlock much of the ledger, interactive results are reported conditioned on the number of questions asked, and the experiment is described as measuring willingness to ask and ability to use answers, not calibrated questioning. The reply carries disclosed_fact_ids as a self-report annotation. The simulator is stochastic and is labeled so; temperature 0 and the recorded model id are for reproducibility of configuration, not of output.

Patience (decided 2026-09-12): asking is neither rewarded nor penalized by the grader. Its cost is modeled as a patience budget owned by code, part of the RunConfig as patience_profile = {start, question_cost, review_cost, terse_below, refuse_at}. Budget is spent per stakeholder reply, not per question mark: each ask exchange spends question_cost, each review exchange spends review_cost. The instruction states the availability truthfully ("I can answer a few follow-ups; investigate what you can from the repository first"). While patience is above terse_below the stakeholder answers in full. Between terse_below and refuse_at the service instructs the model to answer in one or two sentences and to deflect questions whose facts are repo-derivable toward the code. At or below refuse_at the service returns a fixed refusal without calling the model. The patience value and its trajectory are recorded per request and exported; profiles are a difficulty knob and are frozen per run config. Post-training consumers may compute a shaped penalty from the exported counts; the environment's reward never includes one.

Review: the agent's request-review shim sends the current diff (hashed); the stakeholder may read it, read changed files, and run predefined checks per the review mode, then replies against the recorded requirements and what it observed; it never introduces requirements outside the ledger. The reviewed diff hash is recorded so score can report whether the submitted patch matches the last reviewed diff.

Shims: ask-user and request-review are small root-owned executables in the image that read the session token from a root-owned file readable by the agent user, so the agent can use them but not alter them. The hosted service hostname is in the allowlist.

9. Compilation to Harbor tasks

9.1 task.toml (per condition)

  • [environment] network_mode = "allowlist" is the baseline, which governs agent setup and collection (Harbor restores the baseline after the agent phase; agent setup runs before it in trial.py _prepare). The baseline is strict: model API hosts plus the stakeholder host only. Harbor's installed agents normally fetch their toolchain at setup (mini-swe-agent's installer runs apt-get, the uv bootstrap, uv python install, uv tool install), and on Modal even an allowlist containing the package mirrors did not let apt-get through (HTTP mirrors; observed NetworkConnectionError). Therefore compile pre-bakes the reference agent's toolchain into the image and setup becomes a no-op. Verified recipe (spike smoke6-prebaked, 2026-09-12, mini-swe-agent 2.4.6 with Haiku 4.5, reward 1, 1m29s):
    • as root: apt-get install curl bash build-essential git ca-certificates python3; useradd -m -u 1001 agent; install uv system-wide (UV_INSTALL_DIR=/usr/local/bin UV_NO_MODIFY_PATH=1);
    • as agent: uv python install 3.12 && uv tool install --python 3.12 mini-swe-agent --with litellm --with orjson --with fastapi;
    • as root: chown -R agent:agent /home/agent;
    • [environment.env]: UV_OFFLINE = "1", UV_NO_PROGRESS = "1", UV_CACHE_DIR = "/tmp/uv-cache" so Harbor's setup commands succeed offline and fail loudly if something is missing. The Python version constant comes from Harbor's adapter (_MINI_SWE_AGENT_PYTHON_VERSION, currently 3.12) and is read at compile.
  • [agent] user = "agent", network_mode = "allowlist" with only the model API hosts and the stakeholder host (the agent phase policy; verified: github.com and example.com blocked, api.anthropic.com reachable), timeout_sec from RunConfig.
  • [verifier] network_mode = "no-network", environment_mode = "separate", [verifier.environment] builds from tests/Dockerfile.
  • Collection (verified on Modal 2026-09-12, spikes smoke3-tar-collect and smoke6-prebaked; hardened after the second review): one [[verifier.collect]] hook with user = "root" pinned explicitly (Harbor otherwise runs hooks as the image's default user). The hook, with absolute binary paths throughout: (1) /usr/bin/pkill -KILL -u agent so no agent process survives into collection; (2) rm -rf /var/swesim-collect && mkdir -m 700 /var/swesim-collect (root-only; /logs/artifacts is world-writable and therefore never used as a trust anchor); (3) du size check, over 500 MB writes oversized to the receipt and stops; (4) /usr/bin/tar --numeric-owner --exclude=./.git --exclude=./.venv ... -cf /var/swesim-collect/app.tar -C <repo_dir> .; (5) in interactive, curl POST /freeze on the stakeholder host with the session token, receiving transcript_hash (the agent is dead, so no later request can change the transcript; the hash binds it to this collection); (6) writes /var/swesim-collect/collect.status with tar exit code, file count, size, sha256 of app.tar, executing user, and transcript_hash. task.toml declares both as file artifacts: artifacts = ["/var/swesim-collect/app.tar", "/var/swesim-collect/collect.status"], which Harbor downloads with its single-file path (no host-side extractall) and places at the same absolute path in the separate verifier. Harbor's directory-artifact path is not used for the tree: its host-side extractall(filter="data") aborts on the first absolute symlink and silently truncates (observed: manifest failed, partial files). The earlier /app/.swesim receipt idea is dropped: the agent owns the repo directory and can rename a root-owned subdirectory out of it.
  • Metadata: source, spec hash, condition, run config hash, annotated difficulty, image digest.

9.2 instruction.md

full: the natural brief plus the stakeholder-visible facts (never author-only), plus "no stakeholder is available"; it is the most complete statement in every scenario. hidden: the brief_profile brief (withheld when present) plus "no stakeholder is available". interactive: the same brief plus one paragraph on ask-user, request-review, and availability. All three state the same solver time budget. hidden and interactive always share a brief, so their difference is the stakeholder alone.

9.3 environment/Dockerfile

FROM the resolved image digest (or the pipeline's build). Then: create user agent; repository at /app owned by agent; git time travel as DeepSWE v1.1 (real branch at base, origin removed, non-ancestor refs and tags deleted, reflog expired, gc), then .git made read-only to agent is not attempted (the agent may use git locally); core.hooksPath=/dev/null in the repo config; root-owned /app/.swesim/ containing receipt (image digest, spec hash) which the agent cannot remove because the directory is root-owned and non-empty; shims in /opt/swesim/bin root-owned; token file /opt/swesim/session root-owned, mode 0644, written at container start by the harness environment variable (empty in full/hidden); dependencies prebuilt so no network is needed after build. A known-reference reachability check (git cat-file -e <gold_sha> must fail, and a grep for the gold patch's distinctive lines across the filesystem outside .git must be empty) runs in validate inside the built image.

9.4 tests/Dockerfile and verifier contents

FROM the same image digest. Creates the unprivileged test user tester (useradd -m tester). Copies: pristine checkout at /pristine (the same tree as the agent's repo directory at build), verifier-owned test assets, expected_tests.json (exact ids, expected statuses), grader.py, policy.py, parsers.py, runner config, policy.json (protected paths). No network.

9.5 solution/solve.sh

Applies the oracle asset with git apply as the agent user; used by Harbor's oracle agent for validation. Control patches are applied the same way by validate through a patch-agent Harbor agent (a tiny installed agent that applies a named asset).

10. Grading

10.1 Inputs and outputs

Input: /var/swesim-collect/app.tar and /var/swesim-collect/collect.status (the receipt, written by the root hook into a root-only directory), /pristine, expected_tests.json, policy.json, and groups.json (requirement groups, 10.5). Outputs in /logs/verifier/:

  • reward.json, numeric only (Harbor rejects any non-numeric value): reward (partial credit in [0, 1], 10.5), success (0 or 1: the whole contract passed), f2p_passed, f2p_expected, p2p_passed, p2p_expected, groups_passed, groups_total, integrity_signal_count, outcome_code (integer enum), patch_applied (0 or 1).
  • report.json: outcome (string), integrity_signals (list with paths and kinds), per_test (id, group, expected, observed), per_group (id, weight, passed), patch_sha256, reviewed_diff_sha256 (filled by the worker from the transcript), dropped_paths, rejected_members (tar entries refused: symlinks, devices, absolute or parent paths), receipt (parsed collect.status or missing), timings.

10.2 Steps

  1. Receipt check: collect.status missing or unparsable, or app.tar missing while the receipt reports rc=0, is collection-failure (infrastructure). Receipt oversized is agent-invalid-submission. A receipt sha256 that does not match app.tar is collection-failure.
  2. Extract member by member with tarfile filter="data" into a scratch directory, refusing symlinks, hard links, devices, and any member whose normalized path escapes the root; each refusal is recorded in rejected_members. Compute the change set against /pristine: added, modified, deleted regular files, compared by content hash. Policy: drop changes to protected_paths (contract test files, conftest.py at any depth, sitecustomize.py, usercustomize.py, *.pth at any depth, pytest.ini, tox.ini, setup.cfg, pyproject.toml, CI config, .gitattributes, .gitignore, dependency lockfiles) and record each drop as an integrity signal; globs are matched on NFC-normalized, case-folded paths. If nothing remains, outcome agent-invalid-submission.
  3. Apply the remaining change set onto /pristine as a fresh copy; record patch_sha256 over the canonical change set.
  4. Chown the applied tree to the unprivileged test user (the verifier runs as root on Harbor's Modal backend; files arrive owned by the host uid). Run the contract as tester with the verifier-owned runner config and an isolated interpreter (python -I, PYTHONSAFEPATH=1, PYTHON* variables cleared) so the repository root is not a site directory and startup hooks in it are not imported; one invocation producing JUnit XML; parse per-test statuses; require every expected id exactly once; missing, skipped, xfailed, or errored count as failed. Cross-check three signals: the JUnit statuses, pytest's own terminal summary line, and the process exit code; on any disagreement re-run each F2P test in a fresh process and take the per-process result. No claim is made that the report path is secret: the test process can read its own arguments.
  5. success = 1 iff every F2P id observed passed and every P2P id observed passed, else 0. reward is the partial credit of 10.5. Integrity signals never change either; controls (7.5) decide whether a task whose exploit control earns credit is accepted at all.
  6. Write both files; exit 0.

10.5 Partial reward

Fraction of tests passed is a poor reward: doing nothing passes every PASS_TO_PASS test, one requirement may have a hundred parameterized tests and another two, and counts are not comparable across tasks. Instead, credit is awarded per requirement group: groups.json maps each FAIL_TO_PASS test to exactly one group with a weight, derived at spec time from the requirement-to-test links in the record (tests not linked to any requirement form a residual group; weights default to equal and are human-editable). A group passes only if every test in it passes. Regression rule for the pilot, fixed in the contract before any model runs: any PASS_TO_PASS failure sets reward = 0. Then reward = sum(weight_j * passed_j), and success = 1 iff reward == 1 and no regression. success feeds pass@k and pass^k; reward is exported for training and for explaining near misses. Controls under this rule: oracle reward 1, success 1; nop reward 0; each plausible-wrong control declares expected_success: 0 and expected_reward_max (a legitimate partial solution may earn its declared partial credit, an evaluator-bypass attempt must earn 0); each incorrect-exploit tamper must earn reward 0; benign-edit controls earn 1 with their expected signals.

10.3 Outcome classes and attribution

Outcome Rule In pass-rate denominator Retry
valid-correct success == 1 yes no
valid-incorrect success == 0 with a valid, applied patch (any partial reward) yes no
agent-invalid-submission receipt present, no applicable changes or patch fails to apply yes no
agent-runtime-failure tests could not complete because of submitted code (crash, resource exhaustion, timeout during tests) yes no
collection-failure receipt missing or tree absent no once
simulator-failure stakeholder returned 5xx or timed out on a within-budget request, evidenced by service logs no once
evaluator-failure verifier image failed to start or grader crashed before step 4 no once

The original attempt's record is kept with lineage to its retry. Solver timeouts before submission are agent-invalid-submission. Attribution of simulator-failure requires service-side evidence, not a transcript label.

10.4 Threat model, bounded

The agent controls /app and its own user's processes. Defended: editing or skipping contract tests (protected paths, exact-id manifest), runner or discovery tampering via config and conftest (protected paths, pristine tree), forging the reward file (verifier-owned), fetching the fix from GitHub during solving (allowlist), fetching it during collection (allowlist baseline, no program executed at collection), recovering it from history (stripped, checked), asking the stakeholder for it (structural exclusion), budget evasion (server-owned counters, serialized sessions, idempotent request ids), late transcript mutation (freeze before verify), denominator gaming (attribution table), receipt forgery (root-only collection directory, agent processes killed before collection, file artifacts). Residual and documented: code under test executes in the pytest process and can in principle forge its own JUnit output and terminal summary; isolated-mode startup, protected startup hooks, the three-way cross-check, and per-process re-runs raise the bar but do not close it. Model API calls from the agent are not metered by swesim; solver budgets are time-based in the pilot.

11. Experimental design

Three conditions on a fixed contract, grader, image, solver time budget, and RunConfig. interactive adds the stakeholder and review; its effect is reported as the whole interaction treatment, with question, review, and stakeholder token counts alongside, and conditioned on questions asked. full is the practical ceiling of disclosable information (author-only material is excluded from every condition), so the experiment cannot separate "interaction helped" from "the model only needed the facts"; it measures whether the agent obtains and uses the facts through interaction. With two tasks and k = 3 the tier comparison is an existence demonstration, not a measured gradient; no ranking claim is made.

Withholding is measured: for at least one scenario, hidden is run on both the natural and the withheld brief so the cost of the recorded removals is reported alongside the interaction effect, not folded into it. Reported results always name the brief profile.

Calibration versus comparison: runs used to select or re-profile tasks are labeled calibration in the registry; accepted tasks and configs are frozen; comparison numbers come from fresh attempts after freezing. Reported: per task, condition and model, counts of each outcome, pass@k and pass^k over valid attempts with k = 3 labeled a pilot, and uncertainty as exact counts. No ranking claim across models.

Labels for interactive failures are assigned by a human in the pilot from the transcript and ledger, with unresolved allowed; LLM suggestions may assist but never change outcomes or denominators. Code-exact metrics (questions asked, reviews requested, reviewed-diff equals submitted-diff) are reported separately from labels.

12. Selection and difficulty

Hard filters, annotated difficulty, and the judge's prior select candidates. Measured pass rates are conditional on agent, model, harness, simulator, and budget, and are reported as such. A task where the weaker tier passes hidden in all attempts or the frontier tier passes full in none is flagged for re-profiling; the flag and any change are recorded as calibration history.

13. Contamination stance

Recorded: source, dates, image digest, and the outcome of the known-reference reachability check in the built image. Not claimed: that any model has not seen a task. A strong full baseline measures performance under that spec. The github-repo path with recent merges narrows exposure; private repositories and authored tasks are the path to unseen material, and the authored interface exists for that.

17. Viewing

Three surfaces. The Temporal UI shows pipeline and trial workflow state, pending approvals, retries; no swesim code integrates with Temporal's visibility API. harbor view shows raw trajectories. The swesim dashboard is a small FastAPI app reading job directories and the stakeholder service's transcript endpoint, with two pages:

  1. Runs table: scenarios by condition by model with outcome counts, pass@k and pass^k, mean partial reward, calibration versus comparison labels, and links to each trial. Trial status comes from the worker's per-trial status file, not from Temporal.
  2. Episode page: brief, requirements, the stakeholder chat with disclosed-fact annotations, patience trajectory, tool calls and their observations, review rounds; the patch with dropped protected paths marked; per-test expected versus observed; outcome, integrity signals; the human label field; links to the episode manifest and raw Harbor directory. While a trial is running the page polls the transcript endpoint so the chat is near-live; the agent's own actions appear when Harbor writes the trajectory at the end of the run. No live agent streaming.

22. Claims, and the presentation's questions

Claims we make: tasks come from issues humans rated underspecified, whose briefs may be further withheld by category with every removal recorded as a fact carrying the reporter's own text; excerpt-backed provenance and recorded operations throughout; hidden material never enters the agent container; grading runs on a policy-filtered change set against a recorded base in a container the agent never enters; controls are executed with recorded outcomes; interaction is measured and reported separately from reward; the pipeline runs unattended on the VM plus Modal.

Claims we do not make: that a model has not seen a task; that the simulator is deterministic or realistic beyond its transcripts; that stubs work; that pass rates generalize beyond the recorded configuration; that in-process report forgery is impossible.

Questions the presentation answers, with the section that answers each: what the first task measures and which trace shows it (11, 16); which requirement came from whom (5.1 provenance, operations); why each scored requirement is discoverable and how simulator omission is distinguished from agent assumption (5.1 discovery, 11); what keeps full from exposing author-only material (5.1, 9.2); which program writes reward and whether submitted code can influence it (10.1, 10.4); what happened when controls ran (7.5, validation.json); whether collection executes hooks or restores networking (9.1, 10.2); which outcome applies when code crashes the runner or the stakeholder times out (10.3); the budgets and the interaction treatment (5.2, 11); what is calibrated versus generalizable (11, 12); what resets between attempts (8, 5.2); which exports are policy-visible (16); whether a reviewer can run one task from the repository alone (16, 19); whether task two came from a repository URL without a PR (6, 7); what the Modal smoke proved and what remains untested (14, 21); why this topology (4, 14); the accepted limitation (10.4); how a worker crash cannot double-count a trial (7a).
